title: Milestone: How Power Is Shared
objective: After this level you can connect kinds of government, rights and lawmaking into one picture.
summary: A legislator is literally a proposer of a law. Making one law spreads power across legislators, committees, lobbyists, executives, agencies and councils, from Level 1's steering to your street.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Let's see how many hands shape one law.
cards.body: Level 1 said "govern" comes from a Greek word for steering a ship. This chapter showed that in lawmaking, nobody steers alone. Follow one law from a proposal to your street, and count the hands on the wheel.

cards.headline: The proposer of a law
cards.body: A legislator is, literally, a "proposer of a law": the word comes from the Latin legis lator, from lex, law, and lator, one who proposes, from a verb meaning to carry. So a lawmaker's first job isn't deciding. It's proposing, then persuading everyone else. That's why a bill faces readings, debate and committee before Royal Assent turns it into an Act.

cards.headline: Who shares the power over one law?

items.label: Proposing and shaping
points: Committees examine it line by line

items.label: Stopping and filling in
points: An executive can veto; Congress can override by two-thirds
Ministers and agencies write the detailed rules

items.label: Close to home, and over time
points: Councils make byelaws with powers from above
A new act can repeal an old one

mascot.line: Fifty levels in, and you can follow a law from an idea all the way to your street.

cards.headline: Milestone: power shared
learned: A legislator is a "proposer of a law"
Bills pass readings, committees and a possible veto
Ministers, agencies and councils fill in and localize law
Laws can be challenged, obeyed or repealed

questions.prompt: The word "legislator" comes from Latin legis lator. What did that mean?

options.label: Keeper of the peace
options.rationale: The Latin is about law and proposing.

options.label: Reader of the rules
options.rationale: Lator means one who proposes, not one who reads.

options.label: Judge of the people
options.rationale: Judging belongs to courts, not the word's root.

options.label: Proposer of a law

questions.explanation: Legis lator: lex (law) plus lator (proposer), from a verb meaning to carry.

questions.prompt: Making Laws milestone: what do Hammurabi's code and France's Napoleonic Code have in common?

options.label: Both were carved on stone slabs
options.rationale: Only Hammurabi's was engraved in stone.

options.label: Both set the law down as a written code
Both were made by the UK Parliament
options.rationale: Neither came from Westminster.

options.label: Both rely mainly on judges' precedents
options.rationale: That describes common law, not codes.

questions.explanation: Hammurabi had his rulings engraved in writing; the Napoleonic Code of 1804 became a model for the code-based civil law tradition.

questions.prompt: Making Laws milestone: which order is right for a US bill that the President vetoes?

options.label: Both chambers pass it → President vetoes → two-thirds of each override
President vetoes → both chambers pass it → it becomes law
options.rationale: The President acts only after Congress passes the bill.

options.label: House passes it → President signs → Senate may veto it
options.rationale: The veto belongs to the President, and both chambers vote first.

options.label: Both chambers pass it → President vetoes → a simple majority overrides
options.rationale: An override needs two-thirds of each chamber.

questions.explanation: A bill must pass both chambers in identical form, then goes to the President; Congress overrides a veto only by two-thirds of each chamber.

questions.prompt: What does a UK Commons select committee examine about its government department?

options.label: Its spending, policies and administration
Only the department's staff holidays
options.rationale: Its remit is far wider.

options.label: Whether ministers win their elections
options.rationale: Committees examine departments, not election results.

options.label: Nothing: it only writes new bills
options.rationale: Select committees scrutinize how government runs.

questions.explanation: The Commons has a select committee for each department, examining its spending, policies and administration.

questions.prompt: Making Laws milestone: what do a UK minister's statutory instrument and a Leeds byelaw have in common?

options.label: Both need a second reading in the Commons
options.rationale: Neither goes through a bill's stages.

options.label: Both are made by the monarch personally
options.rationale: Ministers and councils make them.

options.label: Both are made using powers granted by Acts of Parliament
Both apply only within one city
options.rationale: Only the byelaw is limited to one area.

questions.explanation: Secondary legislation and byelaws are both delegated lawmaking: made under powers that Acts of Parliament grant.

questions.prompt: Level 7's Locke said people may resist rulers who violate their rights. Which figure from Level 48 chose instead to obey a sentence he thought unjust?

options.label: Henry David Thoreau
options.rationale: Thoreau argued for breaking unjust laws.

options.label: Martin Luther King Jr.
options.rationale: King argued for disobeying unjust laws openly.

options.label: Woodrow Wilson
options.rationale: Wilson wrote about committees, not unjust laws.

options.label: Socrates

questions.explanation: In Plato's Crito, Socrates refuses to escape, arguing he had implicitly agreed to obey Athens's laws.

questions.prompt: Making Laws milestone: ending a Senate filibuster and overriding a US veto both require what?

options.label: A decision by the Supreme Court
options.rationale: Both are votes in Congress, not court rulings.

options.label: The President's signature
options.rationale: Neither needs the President to sign.

options.label: Unanimous agreement
options.rationale: Neither needs every member.

options.label: A supermajority, more than a simple majority

questions.explanation: Cloture needs three-fifths of senators (usually 60); a veto override needs two-thirds of each chamber.
